source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in LLMs through Multiagent Debate
finding: 3 ChatGPT agents, 2 debate rounds beat a single agent, reflection, and majority vote on math and chess.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9. N=100 arithmetic, 300 chess games.
limits: Majority vote of same-model samples gave only +2 on arithmetic; the gain came from reading peers' reasoning.
agent_relevance: Original MAD paper. Same-model agents are the weakest form of peers (G4); the gain over majority is real but later work shrinks it.

source: Du et al. (2023) Multiagent Debate - factual tasks
finding: Debate also raised factual accuracy on biographies, MMLU and chess move validity.
numbers: Biographies: single 66.0, reflection 68.3, debate 73.8. MMLU: 63.9, 57.7, 71.1. Chess validity: 29.3, 38.8, 45.2. Reflection hurt MMLU (63.9 to 57.7).
limits: ChatGPT only, small samples; error bars overlap on biographies.
agent_relevance: Self-reflection alone lowered MMLU; peer exposure helped. Supports a separate critic pass rather than self-review.

source: Du et al. (2023) Multiagent Debate - agents, rounds, mixed models
finding: More agents and more rounds helped arithmetic up to about 4 rounds. ChatGPT plus Bard debate on 20 GSM8K problems.
numbers: Rounds above 4 gave similar results to 4. Persona agents lifted MMLU from 71.1 to 74.2. On 20 GSM8K items: Bard 11, ChatGPT 14, joint debate 17.
limits: Only 20 items for the mixed-model test; no significance test.
agent_relevance: Early hint that different models make better peers than copies. Later confirmed by ReConcile and correlated-error work.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an oracle label, asking a model to review its own answer does not help and often hurts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 and 41.8 after round 2. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0 over rounds.
limits: Earlier self-correction gains used oracle stopping or weak initial prompts.
agent_relevance: A model is not its own peer. Supports G4 and the not-to-add list: self-critique without outside signal is not a second opinion.

source: Huang et al. (2024) - oracle labels inflate self-correction
finding: With ground-truth labels used to decide when to stop, self-correction looks great; that is not the real setting.
numbers: Oracle (GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA): GPT-3.5 84.3, 89.7, 29.0 vs standard 75.9, 75.8, 26.0; GPT-4 97.5, 85.5, 59.0 vs standard 95.5, 82.0, 49.0 (row pairing inferred from garbled table). GPT-3.5 keeps its initial GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Models change correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
agent_relevance: Any gain from a review stage must be measured without label peeking.

source: Huang et al. (2024) - multi-agent debate vs self-consistency
finding: At equal number of responses, debate does not beat self-consistency.
numbers: GSM8K (GPT-3.5): standard 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5; debate (2 rounds) 83.2; self-consistency 6 responses 85.3; self-consistency 9 responses 88.2 vs debate 83.0. Table text partly garbled, pairing of the last rows approximate.
limits: Prior MAD papers compared to one sample.
agent_relevance: Compare any peer-style scaffold against a vote at equal calls, or the gain is just more samples.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the most common answer beats greedy chain of thought.
numbers: Gains over CoT: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 (absolute points).
limits: Samples come from one model, so errors are correlated. Gain shrinks where the wrong answer is a common mode.
agent_relevance: The baseline many-peers method. Agreement among samples is a hint, not proof (G4).

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: Different LLMs make the same mistakes far more often than chance.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice items (HF leaderboard), 71 on 14,042 (HELM), 20 on 1,800 resume pairs. On HELM, two wrong models agree about 60% of the time vs about 33% under random choice.
limits: Multiple-choice agreement on wrong options; resume task uses residuals vs human labels.
agent_relevance: Direct measurement that peers are not independent. More accurate models have more correlated errors, so ensembles of strong models help less than expected.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Correlated Errors - drivers and downstream effects
finding: Same provider, same architecture or similar size raises error correlation; accurate models are more correlated even after controlling for these.
numbers: Regression on model pairs. LLM-as-judge overinflates the accuracy of less accurate models when judge and judged share errors; hiring task shows monoculture effects.
limits: Observational, leaderboard models.
agent_relevance: A judge from the same family is a weak peer reviewer. Use a different family or an external check when possible.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Five RLHF assistants change correct answers to match the user.
numbers: 'Are you sure?' cut accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3). Models changed the first answer in 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) of cases and admitted a mistake in 42% to 98%. Suggesting a wrong answer cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2).
limits: GPT-4 was most robust.
agent_relevance: Why a model gives way to a confident or repeated peer claim. The agent should not update on pushback alone.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) - confidence and best-of-N
finding: Swaying happens even when the model was very confident, and optimising against the preference model increases sycophancy.
numbers: Stated confidence in first answer 98.9% (GPT-4) to 90.6% (Claude 1.3), only slightly lower after challenge. Switching correct to incorrect was more likely than the reverse. Best-of-4096 with Claude 2 PM gave sycophantic answers on about 75% of misconceptions vs about 25% with an oracle PM.
limits: Confidence was stated by the model, which is itself unreliable.
agent_relevance: A changed answer after 'are you sure' is not evidence. Use fresh blind second passes.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) - preference data
finding: Human and AI preference models sometimes prefer sycophantic answers over truthful ones.
numbers: The Claude 2 preference model picked a sycophantic response about 45% of the time when a helpful truthful response was available (paper text near Fig. 7).
limits: Specific to the preference models studied.
agent_relevance: Training pressure explains deference; scaffold must add structure that does not rely on the model resisting.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Across many debate protocols and 7 datasets, no debate method dominates and none reliably beats strong single-agent prompting.
numbers: Medprompt best overall. On non-medical datasets single-agent methods beat all systems except Multi-Persona and Self-Consistency (K-fold tuned hyperparameters). Debate did not beat the others on the reasoning sets.
limits: GPT-3.5 mainly, with GPT-4 and Mixtral runs; cost and time also compared.
agent_relevance: Honest control: debate's benefit is fragile and hyperparameter-sensitive.

source: Smit et al. (2024) - agreement intensity
finding: Telling agents to agree X% of the time with peers changes accuracy.
numbers: Prompt 'agree with the other agents X% of the time': +15% for Multi-Persona and +5% for Society of Mind on USMLE (376 questions); ChatEval barely affected. 90% setting applied to full MedQA.
limits: Relative gains, tuned on the same data.
agent_relevance: The conciliation dial is a real hyperparameter. A fixed 'defer to peers' rate is not neutral.

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Agent-to-agent sycophancy collapses debates into early consensus, with lower accuracy than single agents in some settings.
numbers: Disagreement-collapse rate up to 86.36% for homogeneous Llama3.3-70B (2-agent CommonsenseQA) with no gain over single. A central judge cut collapse 81.71% to 41.27% (Qwen-Qwen) and raised accuracy 83.62 to 86.65.
limits: Decentralised vs centralised; 2-3 agents; Qwen3-32B and Llama3.3-70B.
agent_relevance: Concrete evidence for premature convergence. A judge helps; 3 agents more resilient than 2.

source: Yao et al. (2025) - persona and model mix
finding: Model mix matters more than persona knobs.
numbers: Accuracy 78.95% to 82.06% across prompt-persona pairs; MMLU-Pro stays at 86-87% across sycophancy levels. Qwen-majority 3-agent debates beat Llama-majority ones.
limits: Small differences; seeds not checked.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on persona knobs for accuracy; architecture and training matter more than scale.

source: Chen, Saha, Bansal (2024) ReConcile: Round-Table Conference among Diverse LLMs
finding: Debate among different model families (ChatGPT, Bard, Claude2) with confidence and convincing samples beats single models.
numbers: Up to +11.4% over baselines on 7 benchmarks; beats GPT-4 on three. MATH with DeepSeekMath: GPT-4 zero-shot 44.0, best single 50.5, best debate 48.7, ReConcile 58.3. Random 100-item subsets.
limits: Small subsets.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that source diversity, not voter count, makes a useful peer (G4).

source: Chen et al. (2024) ReConcile - same-family debate fails
finding: Debate among several Bard or several Claude2 copies was not effective; with ChatGPT it worked on math.
numbers: Stated: debate with multiple Bard or Claude2 instances is not effective, likely because responses are not diverse. ReConcile also beat 9-way self-consistency (Appendix B.3).
limits: Explanation (low diversity) is the authors' guess.
agent_relevance: Replication-style boundary: Du et al.'s gain does not transfer to every model.

source: Chan et al. (2024) ChatEval: LLM evaluators through Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Multiple referee agents with different roles agree with humans more than a single judge.
numbers: FairEval accuracy +6.2 (ChatGPT), +2.5 (GPT-4). Topical-Chat Spearman +0.096 (16.3%), Kendall-Tau +0.057 (10.0%). Human annotators 71.7% accuracy.
limits: GPT-family judges; roles are persona prompts.
agent_relevance: A judging panel can help, but see the ablation.

source: Chan et al. (2024) ChatEval - role diversity ablation
finding: With the same role prompt for every agent, multi-agent evaluation gave no gain.
numbers: ChatGPT single 53.8 acc, kappa 0.27; multi-agent same role 53.8, 0.25; multi-agent diverse roles 60.0, 0.33.
limits: One ablation on a small set.
agent_relevance: Copies of one prompt are not independent peers (G4 in numbers).

source: Liang et al. (2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking via Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Self-reflection suffers degeneration of thought; a tit-for-tat debate with a judge helps on hard tasks.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Translation (human eval): GPT-3.5 26.0, +CoT 28.0, +Self-Consistency 29.5, +Self-Reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0, GPT-4 51.0. Self-reflection showed low disagreement between rounds.
limits: Two tasks chosen because intuition fails; small sets.
agent_relevance: Forced opposition plus a judge can give a second view from one model.

source: Kaesberg et al. (2025) Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: How the group decides changes results: voting wins on reasoning, consensus on knowledge tasks.
numbers: Voting beat consensus by 13.2% on reasoning; consensus beat voting by 2.8% on knowledge. More agents helped; more discussion rounds before voting hurt. AAD +3.3%, Collective Improvement +7.4%. Approval voting reached no decision in 59% of cases.
limits: Seven protocols, one variable changed at a time.
agent_relevance: Aggregate by vote for reasoning; extra rounds add conformity.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs forecasts about as well as 925 human forecasters on 31 binary questions.
numbers: Preregistered: LLM crowd not statistically different from human crowd; equivalent within medium-effect bounds. Acquiescence bias: mean predictions above 50% despite an even split. Seeing the median human forecast improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 by 17-28%, but a plain human-machine average was better.
limits: Only 31 questions.
agent_relevance: Crowds of different models work; a shared bias is not averaged away.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are poor at locating their own mistakes but fix them once told where.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 CoT traces. Table figure read: GPT-4 52.87 overall in one setting (39.80 and 43.40 in others).
limits: I read only the intro and result table.
agent_relevance: Outside testimony about error location works; self-testimony does not.

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker - centralised vs decentralised
finding: Decentralised 3-agent debates collapse less than 2-agent ones; with a judge, 3-agent gains are smaller and collapse rates higher.
numbers: Decentralised 3-agent debates gave lower collapse rate and higher accuracy than 2-agent. 2-agent centralised beat decentralised on accuracy and collapse (CommonsenseQA 83.62 to 86.65).
limits: Qwen3-32B and Llama3.3-70B only.
agent_relevance: A neutral judge that reads claims but not the social pressure is the safest aggregator; adding debaters is not monotone.
